claims.text: Protective oxide formation and retention in high-entropy alloys is governed by selective surface enrichment of reactive elements such as Al or Cr during high-temperature exposure.
Sluggish diffusion and lattice distortion inherent to a disordered multi-element matrix drive reactive-element surface segregation.
Reactive-element surface enrichment preferentially produces stable Al2O3 or Cr2O3 phases.
Reactive-element enrichment leads to a continuous oxide film.
Reactive-element enrichment leads to an adherent oxide film.
A continuous dense oxide layer inhibits further oxidation by acting as a diffusion barrier to oxygen ingress.
Differences in elemental diffusivities at elevated temperature govern reactive-element redistribution.
Al or Cr diffuses more slowly within the complex matrix and consequently accumulates at the alloy surface.
Increasing the reactive-element concentration causes the protective oxide layer to form earlier than in a lower-concentration baseline.
Increasing the reactive-element concentration produces a more continuous oxide film than in a lower-concentration baseline.
Increasing the reactive-element concentration produces a more adherent oxide film than in a lower-concentration baseline.
Increasing the reactive-element concentration lowers the overall oxidation rate relative to the baseline.
Increasing the reactive-element concentration improves oxide-scale uniformity and density relative to the baseline.
The proposed mechanism applies in oxygen-rich environments between approximately 800 and 1100 °C.
Formation of volatile CrO3 above 900 °C can become sufficiently important to invalidate the proposed mechanism.
The starting alloys are homogeneous disordered solid solutions with initially uniform reactive-element distributions.
A dense Al-containing oxide layer can remain protective during 50–100 hours of oxidation at 800 °C.
